content.title: About
content.content: Caribou is a premium dry blend of selected cranberry and seaweed, enriched with B‑vitamins and minerals. It is designed to support energy levels and immune function during high physical demand.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Caribou formula was developed together with nutritionists and athletes.
Seaweed adds iodine, which supports normal thyroid function.
Its low glycemic index makes Caribou suitable for people monitoring blood sugar.
The product is free from gluten, lactose, and artificial sweeteners.
Packaging is made from recyclable material and is fully recyclable.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C and antioxidants from cranberry help strengthen the body’s defenses.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: Complex carbs and B‑vitamins provide a steady release of energy.

items.title: Thyroid health
items.content: Iodine from seaweed supports normal thyroid hormone production.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Cranberry fiber promotes regular bowel function.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Cranberry flavonoids help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Seaweed allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seaweed components.

items.title: Excess iodine
items.content: Consuming large amounts may lead to iodine overload, which is undesirable for thyroid disorders.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although the glycemic index is low, the product contains natural cranberry sugars; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Caribou can be eaten as a dry snack, mixed into yogurt, smoothies, oatmeal, or sprinkled over salads. The recommended serving is 30 g per day, taken with water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Caribou in a dry, cool place with the package tightly sealed. For long‑term storage (over 6 months) keep it refrigerated.

chicken-thigh-baked-coated-skin-coating-.title: Chicken thigh, baked, coated, skin / coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is dark meat that is flavorful and nutrient‑dense. When baked in the oven with a coating (breaded) but without eating the skin or coating, the meat retains its core nutrients while excess fat is reduced.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
Baking without the skin lowers saturated fat while keeping the thigh juicy.
Coatings can be made from whole‑grain flour, breadcrumbs, or nut meals, adding texture and aroma.
Chicken thighs are a staple in many cuisines, from French coq au vin to Asian teriyaki.
Proper cooking yields tender meat with a crisp, golden crust.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Dark meat supplies more heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Thighs without skin or edible coating contain virtually no carbs, fitting low‑carb diets.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Chicken must reach an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F) to eliminate salmonella.

items.title: Allergy to coating ingredients
items.content: If the coating contains gluten, nuts, or dairy, allergic reactions are possible.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared breadings often contain salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Fat from accidental skin consumption
items.content: While the skin is not meant to be eaten, accidental consumption adds saturated fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the thighs as a main dish, slice them for salads, add to soups, or place in sandwiches. Let them rest a few minutes after baking so the crust stays crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked thighs in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in sealed bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Gnocchi with cheese are Italian potato dumplings that are boiled or pan‑fried and mixed with melted cheese. Traditional gnocchi are made from cooked potatoes, flour and eggs, while the cheese adds a creamy, savory flavor. The dish is popular as a light dinner or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gnocchi originate from northern Italy, where they are sometimes called "little knots".
There are more than 200 variations of gnocchi, including pumpkin, spinach and whole‑grain versions.
Typical cheeses used are Parmesan, mozzarella or Gorgonzola, depending on the region.
In Italy gnocchi are often served with tomato sauce, cream sauce or simply butter and sage.
Homemade gnocchi are easy to make: boil potatoes, mash them, add flour and shape small "pillows".

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Potatoes provide slow‑releasing energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: The cheese contributes a good amount of calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Combined potato and cheese deliver a complete set of essential amino acids.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Gnocchi contain vitamins B6 and B12, supporting nervous system function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Using whole‑grain flour increases fiber content, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese may cause discomfort for people who cannot digest lactose.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Cheese‑filled gnocchi are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Many cheeses are salty, which can be an issue for those with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional flour contains gluten, making the dish unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot gnocchi with cheese, topped with extra cheese and fresh herbs. They can be added to soups, baked in the oven with tomato sauce, or enjoyed as a standalone dish with olive oil and spinach.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Dry gnocchi keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 3 days. Cooked gnocchi with cheese should be cooled and refrigerated for no more than 2 days. For longer storage, freeze on a tray and then transfer to a bag; they stay good for about a month.

content.title: About
content.content: Italian dressing, fat free, is a flavorful sauce made from vinegar, lemon juice, herbs, and spices, with all oils removed. It retains the classic Italian dressing taste while providing virtually no fat and very few calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The fat‑free version was created in response to growing demand for diet‑friendly condiments.
Its classic flavor comes from a blend of oregano, basil, garlic, and onion.
Mustard powder is often added to boost aroma without adding fat.
The dressing is suitable for vegetarians and vegans.
It can be used not only on salads but also as a marinade for vegetables and seafood.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The absence of oil makes this dressing an excellent choice for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Herbs such as oregano and basil contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Vinegar and lemon juice stimulate gastric juice production, aiding food digestion.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Lemon juice provides a modest amount of vitamin C, which supports immune function.

items.title: No trans fats
items.content: Without added oils, there is no risk of consuming trans fats that can harm cardiovascular health.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions may be high in salt, which should be considered by people with hypertension.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Individuals may react to mustard, garlic, or onion.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in those with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drizzle over salads, vegetable mixes, seaweed salads, or use as a marinade for chicken, fish, and tofu. It can also be added to soups for a light tang.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated in a tightly sealed container. Once opened, use within 2–3 weeks. Discard if the smell or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Oatmeal is a ready‑to‑eat product made from whole oat grains, designed for fast preparation in fast‑food settings. It is typically steamed, dried and flavored with varieties such as berry, chocolate or vanilla.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown for over 5,000 years.
Instant oatmeal is often fortified with B‑vitamins and iron.
Flavorings can be natural (berries, nuts) or artificial, but always pass safety checks.
Oatmeal in fast‑food is commonly served in single‑serve cups for on‑the‑go convenience.
Oats contain beta‑glucans, which help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Oatmeal provides soluble fiber that supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Lowers cholesterol
items.content: Beta‑glucans in oats can reduce LDL (bad) cholesterol.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: It delivers steady energy without rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Contains vitamins and minerals
items.content: Includes B1, magnesium, iron and zinc, important for metabolism.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Regular oatmeal consumption is linked to a reduced risk of heart disease.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oats or added flavorings.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Flavored versions often contain added sugars, increasing calorie count.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Oats can be contaminated with wheat during processing, so people with celiac disease should choose certified gluten‑free options.

items.title: Overconsumption
items.content: Convenient portion sizes can lead to eating more than recommended, potentially causing weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the oatmeal in the microwave or with hot water for 1–2 minutes, then add fruit, nuts, honey or yogurt. It can be used as a quick breakfast, snack, or dessert base.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place away from direct light. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and consume within 2–3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Wonton is a traditional Asian dish consisting of a thin dough wrapper filled with vegetables, mushrooms or tofu and deep‑fried until golden and crispy. The meat‑free version is popular among vegetarians and anyone looking for a light yet satisfying snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wontons originate from Chinese cuisine, where they are often called “fried dumplings”.
The dough is made from flour, water and sometimes egg, giving it elasticity and a crunchy texture after frying.
Across Asia, wontons are served with a variety of dipping sauces: soy, vinegar, chili, or aromatic ginger sauce.
Fried wontons are a common appetizer in sushi bars and Asian‑fusion restaurants.
Meat‑free wontons can be easily adapted with tofu, mushrooms, carrots, cabbage or soy crumble.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When fried in a modest amount of vegetable oil, wontons retain a moderate fat content, mostly polyunsaturated.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Tofu or soy‑based fillings provide a complete amino‑acid profile useful for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough and soy ingredients contain thiamine, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetable fillings such as cabbage, carrots and mushrooms add fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Whole‑grain dough and the absence of added sugars make fried wontons suitable for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Tofu and soy crumble can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium in sauces
items.content: Traditional soy sauces are salty; choose low‑sodium versions when possible.

items.title: Frying oil concerns
items.content: Over‑frying can create trans fats; it’s best to fry at the right temperature with a small amount of oil.

items.title: Temperature control
items.content: Undercooked wontons may stay soft inside, affecting texture and increasing bacterial risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot with soy, vinegar, or chili dipping sauce. Wontons can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, soups, or packed in bento boxes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked wontons in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a separate bag – they retain flavor and crunch for up to 2 months. Re‑heat by pan‑frying or baking.
